name: Naqada culture (Predynastic Egypt)
summary: The Copper Age culture of Upper Egypt that came just before the pharaohs. Its leaders, crafts and early hieroglyphs led directly to the unification of Egypt around 3100 BCE.

location.value: Upper Egypt along the Nile, named after the town of Naqada, later spreading to the delta.
location.source: Wikipedia: Naqada culture (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

terrain.value: The narrow, fertile Nile valley between dry deserts.
terrain.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

climate.value: The Sahara was drying, pushing people closer to the Nile.
climate.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

resources.value: Nile floodplain soil, flint, stone for vessels and gold from the Eastern Desert.
resources.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

disasters.value: Variable Nile floods: too high or too low could cause famine.
disasters.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

population.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

urbanisation.value: Towns such as Naqada, Hierakonpolis and Abydos grew with temples and elite cemeteries.
urbanisation.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

disease.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

migration.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

economicBase.value: Farming of wheat and barley, cattle herding and specialised crafts.
economicBase.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Nubia, the Levant and Mesopotamia (lapis lazuli from Afghanistan reached Egypt).
tradeRoutes.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; rich tombs show a growing elite.
wealth.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

moneyAndTax.value: No money; goods were exchanged and stored.
moneyAndTax.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

inequality.value: Rich elite tombs with fine goods show growing inequality.
inequality.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

governmentType.value: Chiefdoms that grew into small kingdoms, then “Dynasty 0” kings.
governmentType.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

keyRulers.value: “Dynasty 0” rulers such as Scorpion and Narmer, who is often credited with unifying Egypt.
keyRulers.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

succession.value: Unknown; probably hereditary chiefs in later phases.
succession.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

institutions.value: Early royal symbols such as the crowns and the serekh (royal name box).
institutions.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

stability.value: Lasted about 700 years (about 3800–3100 BCE, Naqada I–III).

eliteConflict.value: Competing centres such as Naqada, Hierakonpolis and Abydos.
eliteConflict.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

armyAndTech.value: Maceheads, flint knives, bows and arrows.
armyAndTech.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

majorWars.value: Wars between rival centres before Egypt was unified.
majorWars.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

territoryChange.value: Naqada culture spread north into Lower Egypt by about 3200 BCE.
territoryChange.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

alliancesRivals.value: The Lower Egyptian (Maadi-Buto) cultures in the north.
alliancesRivals.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

inventions.value: Early hieroglyphs on labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (about 3200 BCE).
inventions.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

scienceEducation.value: The beginnings of writing and record-keeping.
scienceEducation.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

openness.value: Took ideas from Mesopotamia, such as cylinder seals and some art motifs.
openness.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

communicationTransport.value: The Nile was the main road: boats with oars and, by Naqada II, sails; donkeys on land.

religion.value: The page says only that figurines found beside bodies at Naqada sites may point to mortuary use, and that early African beliefs were the root of Egyptian ways of life. It does not mention gods in art.

languageWriting.value: Early Egyptian, with the first hieroglyphs late in the period.
languageWriting.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

artsArchitecture.value: Painted pottery with boats, the Gebel el-Arak knife, and the Hierakonpolis tomb painting.
artsArchitecture.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

socialStructure.value: Elite rulers, skilled craftspeople and farmers.
socialStructure.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Upper Egyptian culture that spread north.
sharedIdentity.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

dailyLife.value: Houses of reeds and mud, later mud brick; bread and beer from emmer wheat and barley, fish from the Nile; linen clothing.

neighbours.value: Lower Egypt, Nubia (the A-Group) and the Levant.
neighbours.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

ideasReligions.value: Early royal ideas and symbols later used by the pharaohs.
ideasReligions.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

colonisation.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

peakPeriod.value: The page dates Naqada I to about 3900–3650 BCE, Naqada II to 3650–3300 and Naqada III to 3300–2900, so the entry’s 3200–3100 is only part of the last phase.

declineSignals.value: Not a decline: it merged into the first Egyptian dynasty.
declineSignals.source: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

outcome.value: Ended about 3100 BCE with the unification of Egypt.

overallCertainty.value: Medium; the border map shows it earlier than dating suggests.

knownFor.label: Decorated pottery
knownFor.note: Pots painted with boats and animals.

knownFor.label: Early hieroglyphs
knownFor.note: Labels from tomb U-j at Abydos.
